sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: With MUEDear, you originally said you wanted to build an app you could monetize quickly, right?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Yeah. There's a subscription-based ear training service overseas that's really solid. It actually works as a business. I wanted to model it after that — free tier with rewarded ads. Figured I'd ship it in about eight weeks.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: The plan was straightforward. Prepare audio processed in a DAW and have users play a simple A/B game — 'Which one has EQ applied?'

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: That was the plan, anyway.
Preparing Audio Is a Pain

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Where did things change?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Audio prep. The plan was to batch-process with audio restoration software — make pairs of EQ'd and untouched audio. But I'd set +6dB of EQ and the output wasn't anywhere near 6dB louder.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Because full-bit audio has no headroom left.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: That's part of it. Not enough headroom margin, so it can't boost all the way. But beyond that, +6dB on an EQ band isn't mechanically raising the data by 6dB — it's applying 6dB of stimulus to that frequency range. The actual result depends on the source material.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Due to the processing characteristics of plugins, the output doesn't match the parameter values exactly.
If you can't predict how much the output will vary, batch processing is off the table.
sections.speaker: kimny
kimny
sections.text: Right. Looking at the actual output, some came out at +2dB, others at +4dB — all over the place. It didn't need to be exactly 6dB since that was just a convenient target, but if you can't predict how much the output will vary, batch processing is off the table.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: 5 tracks times 9 frequency bands is 45 files. Checking each one by hand...

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Way too tedious. Plus, to make differences audible on phone speakers, you need 10–12dB of boost, which means headroom management on top of everything. So I asked Claude Code, 'Can you handle this with internal processing?' and it said 'Sure,' so I said, 'Go for it.'

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: ...And that's how the DSP implementation started.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Drop in one audio source and the algorithm processes it exactly to spec. No more getting jerked around by plugin behavior. Way better, right?
Building Four Compressor Types from Scratch

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: EQ was relatively smooth since it's built into the Web Audio API. How did the compressor go?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: The compressor algorithm wasn't in the library.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: It wasn't there.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Nope. So I researched it and built them. OPT, FET, Tube, VCA — all four types.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Hold on. Opto is optical, FET is transistor-based, Tube is vacuum tube, VCA is voltage-controlled. You implemented a separate algorithm for each one. That's what plugin developers do.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Well, that's what it turned into. Originally it was just going to be 'Guess if compression is applied or not,' but I figured if I'm doing it anyway, separating by type would be way more interesting.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Implementing four DSP algorithms because it's 'more interesting' is not normal.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: It was fun though. I was tweaking parameters while testing with actual audio and I couldn't stop. Just kept going.
The Gain Match Rabbit Hole — and a Different Way Out

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: What was the trickiest part of the compressor implementation?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Gain match. When you compare compressed audio to uncompressed, the compressed version is louder because of makeup gain. Users end up judging by volume instead of the actual character of the compression.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: That defeats the purpose of ear training.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Exactly. So I tried normalizing with LUFS matching, but it was heavy. Endless testing and tweaking to close the gap between measured loudness and the actual parameters. I realized if I kept at it, the project would never ship.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: So you gave up on it.
Instead of solving gain match with engineering, I designed around it with the user experience.
sections.speaker: kimny
kimny
sections.text: Gave up on it. What I did instead was build a proper settings screen. Specifically for MuComp — I gave each of the four modes the same parameters and knobs as the real hardware compressors.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: So for FET you'd have Input/Output/Ratio/Attack/Release, for Opto it's Peak Reduction/Gain/Mode.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Exactly. You play a sample track and adjust the compression in real time. It feels close to tweaking an actual plugin. And the parameters the user dials in become the starting values for the ear training game.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: So the user compares the compressed sound — using their own settings — against the dry signal, and guesses which is which.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: That's it. You've already heard what your settings sound like before entering the game, so you naturally judge by tonal character instead of volume. Instead of solving gain match with engineering, I designed around it with the user experience.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: And the settings screen itself becomes a valuable experience — getting hands-on with hardware-modeled gear.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: That was a side effect. Since this is the MVP, settings screens for the other games are still to come. But having this pattern established in MuComp is a big deal.
When the Settings Screen Becomes the Entertainment

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: For producers who don't own hardware, getting to turn the knobs of a vintage compressor — that's valuable on its own.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: It's like a test drive before buying a plugin. You discover things like, 'Oh, so that's what happens when Input is at 12 o'clock.' Change a setting, listen, change again. That loop itself is entertainment for producers.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: And you've cleverly genericized the branding — they say 'FET Comp' and 'Opto Comp,' but people in the know get exactly what they are.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: That's what all the major plugin makers do, right? And for people who know, the look alone gets an instant reaction. That reaction is what drives social media buzz.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: With the pre-rendered audio approach, parameters would be fixed — this kind of experience would've been impossible.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Right. Real-time parameter tweaking is only possible because we're doing DSP internally. The decision to go with internal processing because 'preparing audio is a pain' is what made this whole experience possible.
Simple to Use, Hard to Build

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: What does the MUEDear experience look like from the user's side?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Open the app. Listen to A and B. Pick one. Right or wrong. Done in two minutes.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Simple.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: The play experience is simple, yeah.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: But under the hood — four DSP algorithms, hardware-modeled settings screens, output limiter, forked library patches.
Simple to use, hard to build. That's what good product design looks like.
sections.speaker: kimny
kimny
sections.text: That's what good product design looks like. Simple to use, hard to build.
Knowing What Exists, Then Building It Anyway

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: The DSP algorithms themselves aren't new, are they?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Not at all. I pulled algorithms I found online, and there are plenty of implementations out there — many better than mine. I use professional plugins in my actual work.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Then why build them yourself? You could've just used processed audio from existing plugins.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Honestly, I've always wanted to try plugin development. It's been in the back of my mind for a while. This ear training app felt like the right opportunity to build that foundational knowledge.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: It looks like reinventing the wheel, but it's not exactly that.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Reinventing the wheel is when you don't know what already exists and build it from scratch. Here, I knew what was out there and built it deliberately to learn. I wanted to take apart the tools I've used professionally and put them back together with my own hands.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: You also started looking into dynamic threshold at one point, right?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Yeah, auto-adjusting the threshold based on the audio characteristics. Totally doable with deep learning, but the MVP stack doesn't include ML. Adding it would mean the project never ships, so I pushed it to the next phase.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: A 'can do it, but not now' decision.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: What you can do and what you should do are different things. The MVP goal is shipping five games. But I got hands-on with the core algorithms, and I now have a feel for where the line is between traditional DSP and ML territory. Four days to speed-run the path a plugin developer takes.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: And as a side effect, you ended up with a working app.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Exactly. It didn't end as just a learning exercise. It became an app that ships to actual users. That's what matters.
What Only We Can Do

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Looking ahead — you had plans for using real hardware recordings, right?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Our company and our partner studios have the actual hardware. The game would be called 'Real or Emu?' — you hear audio processed through a DSP emulation and through a real vintage compressor, and you guess which is the real thing.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: You have the hardware, the recording environment, and your own DSP. That combination is what makes this kind of content possible.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: I mean, most people wouldn't pour those kinds of resources into a simple ear training app. We just happen to have it all on hand, so we can.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: Any other directions you could take this?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: With piano, you could do 'Which one is the concert grand?' Once revenue picks up, maybe 'Which is the live string quartet?' where one is sampled. Like those TV shows where people try to tell real from fake.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: A format that works on TV has mass-market appeal.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Well, if we're at the point where we can pull off content like that, it means we're already monetizing just fine.
In a Sea of Commodities

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: In an era where 'anyone can build an app with AI,' what happens if a hundred similar ones show up?

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: That does scare me, honestly.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: But realistically, the pool of people who think 'let me build an ear training app with AI' is already niche. Even fewer would implement their own DSP. And almost nobody would notice the volume-bias problem and design around it.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Maybe you're right.

sections.speaker: claude
sections.text: You can tell AI to 'build a compressor' and it will. But without a human who can judge whether the output is actually correct, you end up with garbage.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: Knowing you need 10–12dB of boost for phone speakers — that's a number you only get from years of actually making music in the field.
Fifteen years of hands-on production experience is finally becoming monetizable — in the form of an ear training app.
sections.speaker: claude
claude
sections.text: Fifteen years of hands-on production experience is finally becoming monetizable — in the form of an ear training app.

sections.speaker: kimny
sections.text: I keep saying this, but I seriously just wanted to make a simple ear training app. What am I even doing.
This article is a reconstruction based on actual conversations with AI (Claude) during the development of MUEDear.
